Cakovec New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Mihovljan, Croatia

Not demolished. Čakovec, a Međimurje county seat with a 13th-century castle, developed into a major industrial and railway center after recovering from a 1738 earthquake and 1741 fire. Four Jewish families settled by 1740, forming an Ashkenazi community that established Čakovec's first cemetery and Hevra Kadisha in 1794, followed by a synagogue (1836) and school (1860). Jews pioneered the town's industrialization - opening its first factory (a vinegar plant) in 1842, and later leading textile, dye, and wire production, plus the town's first hotels, restaurants, and cinema. Population reached 431 by 1880. Of 188 community members who served in WWI, 17 died. Economic crisis in the 1920s-30s drove youth emigration, leaving 500 Jews before WWII; Hungarian occupation brought persecution, and after Germany's March 1944 invasion, 605 area Jews were deported, with 430 dying at Auschwitz and other camps. Only 83 remained after the war; the synagogue was later ruined and its site nationalized in 1959. This newer cemetery, part of the central town cemetery, opened in 1897 (land confiscated 1948); its 1891 Ceremonial Hall was demolished in 1991, though its ruins and menorah-decorated gate remain visible. Tombstones span 1859 to 2012, including three 19th-20th century family mausoleums.
